idiom_name: governor RateLimiter (GCRA) - direct and keyed limiters
implementation_notes: In Rust the canonical dedicated crate is governor, which implements the Generic Cell Rate Algorithm and keeps state compactly: RateLimiter::direct(quota) meters one stream, RateLimiter::keyed(quota) keeps one state per key, and Quota::per_second names the limit. check() and check_key() are the cheap synchronous decisions returning NotUntil on refusal, while the middleware module (RatelimitedSink/RatelimitedStream) and the prelude traits adapt the limiter to async code. The crate is no_std-friendly, and because the state is in-process it must be combined with a shared store when the limit spans hosts.
pitfalls: Keyed limiters retain one state entry per key: unbounded key cardinality (IPs, tokens) leaks memory unless entries are evicted.
The limiter is per process; a cluster of services each admits the full quota against the shared dependency.
check() is non-blocking by design; code that must wait needs the async middleware or an explicit delay, not a busy-wait loop on check().

variants.name: tower RateLimit middleware
variants.implementation_notes: In a tower/hyper async service stack the limiter is a layer: RateLimitLayer::new(num, per) wraps a Service and enforces a maximum number of requests per period per wrapped instance, composed via ServiceBuilder alongside timeouts and load shedding. That keeps the policy in the middleware stack shared by every route using it; it is neither per-client nor distributed, so per-key limits still need governor or a shared store in front.
pitfalls: The layer limits the service instance it wraps, not a client: per-caller limits need keyed state (governor) or an external store.
Layer order changes the semantics - a limiter placed after load shedding never sees the shed traffic.
Over-limit requests are refused with the layer's own error type, which the service must map to a refusal response instead of a generic 500.
